children.text: Start With the Register

The previous lesson made the case for a portfolio office. This one is the first thing that office should do in its first month: build the register and run the sequencing test against it. Neither step needs software, a consultant, or a budget line. Both need someone with the standing to ask every department what it is running, and the discipline to write the answers down in one place.

PMI's Standard for Portfolio Management treats portfolio definition as the foundational act: every component identified, classified, and assigned governance. Vermont has never published such a definition, so the book's Chapter 15 assembled one by reading Act 68, the AHEAD State Agreement, the Rural Health Transformation Program application, and the AHS transformation reports for every initiative carrying a named owner and a dated obligation. The exercise produced nineteen components across the five pillars. That number is not the point; the method is.

A register entry needs five fields, and each one does work. The pillar tells you which gate the component sits behind. The owner tells you who answers for it. The type separates compliance projects from strategic programs. The status says whether it is not started, in design, implementing, or done. And the calendar target records the statutory or contractual date — which, as the rest of this lesson shows, is the field you should trust least when deciding what to work on next.

Expect the register to move. Vermont withdrew from the AHEAD State Agreement in July 2026, which turned one component from a live program into a closeout obligation, and hospital transformation plans moved from submission to implementation after final plans were due in March 2026. A register that is not revisited at every governance review quietly becomes a record of last year's portfolio.

A portfolio register is not a status report. A status report lists what is happening. A register lists everything that has to happen, who owns it, and which pillar it depends on — so that the question "what should we work on next?" can be answered by dependency rather than by deadline.

children.text: The Four Steps, Turned Into Verdicts

The book's sequencing test asks four questions of every component, in order. Which pillar does it belong to? Is that pillar's upstream gate open? If the gate is closed, what is gating it, and is that resourced? If the gate is open, is this component actually running? The definition of an open gate comes from Chapter 1: open means the enabling work is finished, not that a milestone was declared.

Run against a register, those four questions produce a small set of verdicts, and the vocabulary matters because it changes the conversation. A component behind a closed gate that has not started is not "behind schedule" — it is correctly waiting. A component with nothing upstream holding it that has not started is late, even if its deadline is two years away. A component implementing while its gate is closed is spending money on output nobody can use yet.

Two qualifications come from Chapter 1 and keep the test from becoming a blunt instrument. First, design never waits for a gate: specifying what a payment model must measure is precisely what tells the technology build what to deliver, so Economics-as-design runs in parallel with the Technology stage. Second, some components produce value on their own. The book says Blueprint PCMH expansion, CCBHC certification, and Collaborative Care deployment proceed in parallel with Technology work — correctly — because they deliver value whether or not the downstream gates have opened.

Notice what the test does not use: the deadline. Calendar targets stay in the register because statutes and grants impose them, and a portfolio office has to report against them. But a verdict that changed with the deadline would just be the old status report under a new name. The test is useful precisely because two components with the same due date can receive opposite verdicts — one correctly waiting, one already late.
Only implementation waits for a gate. Design work, and care-model work that produces value on its own, should be running now.

children.text: Worked Example: Vermont, Fall 2026

Load the book's nineteen components with their Fall 2026 statuses into the platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test and use the same gate profile the HTR Simulator uses for Vermont: the Policy gate open on the strength of Acts 167, 51, and 68, and Technology only partly delivered. The Economics gate is therefore not open. The AHS-GMCB analytics vendor, which the book records as in procurement with a January 2027 operational target, is not yet running — and AHS reported in March 2026 that an analytics contract for regional planning was still under negotiation.

The test then sorts the portfolio. Thirteen components are on track. Two Economics components — RBP implementation and global-budget design and implementation — are in design, which is exactly what Chapter 1 says they should be doing while the Technology gate is closed. One, the Vermont CIN build-out, sits behind an open gate but is still only in design. Two are late by dependency order despite distant deadlines: the statewide AI-governance framework, which nothing upstream is holding, and — pointedly — the AHS PMO itself.

One component is flagged as running ahead of its gate: RHT Program deployment, which the book places in the Economics pillar and describes as active. That is not a verdict that the money is wasted. It is a prompt to ask which parts of the deployment depend on analytics that do not yet exist, and to hold those parts until they do. Finally, step three of the test names where schedule pressure belongs: the four unfinished Technology components, each of which holds the same three gated Economics components behind it.

children.text: What Happens When Nobody Owns the Sequence

The sequencing test assumes someone has the authority to act on its answers — to hold a component back, or to move resources to the one that gates everything else. The clearest public record of what happens without that authority comes from two health-insurance marketplace launches in 2013, each investigated afterward in detail.

The federal Office of Inspector General's case study of HealthCare.gov found that the most critical misstep was the absence of clear leadership, which delayed decisions, and that there was no entity serving formally as systems integrator to coordinate the separately contracted pieces of the build. It also documented poor coordination between policy and technical work and resistance to hearing bad news. Oregon, building its own exchange, made a structurally similar choice and did not recover.

body.content:
The HHS Office of Inspector General's February 2016 case study (OEI-06-14-00350) found that the "absence of clear leadership" delayed decisionmaking, and that no entity was formally serving as systems integrator to coordinate key functions built by different contractors.
After the failed October 2013 launch, CMS hired QSSI as technical systems integrator to coordinate technical tasks and resources, and the OIG reports that CMS recovered the website for high consumer use within two months — once one party owned the integration.
body.title: HealthCare.gov (federal marketplace, 2013)

body.content:
An independent review by First Data, commissioned by Governor John Kitzhaber and based on 67 interviews and more than 3,200 documents, found that Oracle had been hired on a time-and-materials basis, which contributed to a lack of scope control, delayed requirements, and unrealistic delivery expectations. "A system integrator with a stronger financial incentive for ensuring performance most likely would have pushed harder," the review said.
On April 25, 2014, Cover Oregon's board voted to abandon its own enrollment site and move to HealthCare.gov.
body.title: Cover Oregon (state marketplace, 2013–2014)

children.text: The lesson for a state portfolio is not that contractors are the problem. Vermont's own March 2026 Act 68 report lists contracted transformation support, a new hospital technical-assistance vendor, and an analytics contract under negotiation — sensible ways to add capacity. The question both marketplace reviews raise is different: when those contractors' deliverables depend on one another, who decides which one waits? A contractor delivers a defined scope. Only an owner with authority over the whole portfolio can hold one component back so that another can finish first.
Most critical was the absence of clear leadership, which caused delays in decisionmaking. — HHS Office of Inspector General, HealthCare.gov case study, 2016
Reading Risk Alongside Sequence

Chapter 15's risk register scores each risk as probability times impact. Two risks tie for the top score of 20: the analytics vendor not being operational by January 2027 (R-01), and portfolio-management infrastructure not being established before the 2027 deadlines (R-10). The sequencing test and the register point at the same place — the analytics gate — from two directions, which is a useful cross-check: if your pressure points and your highest risks disagree, one of the two is wrong.

The register also shows why a moderate risk score is not a licence to wait. Social-risk adjustment not being adopted before the FY2028 budgets (R-08) scores 12 — a medium probability times a high impact. Yet the sequencing test says this methodology has no upstream blocker and should already be running. Treating it as a FY2028 problem because that is when it is due is the scheduling error that leaves equity work perpetually late.

In practice, bring both artifacts to the same governance meeting. Start with the components that appear in both places — a pressure point in the sequencing test that also carries a top-scored risk. Those are the decisions the board should make first, and they are usually few. Then look for the opposite pattern: unblocked work with a middling risk score and a distant deadline. That is where equity and governance work tends to hide, because nothing on either list makes it feel urgent.

body.title: Two ways to read the same portfolio

children.text: Run It on Your Own Portfolio

The platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test takes either Vermont's register or yours. Start a blank register, enter your components with their pillar and status, and decide for each one whether its implementation genuinely depends on the upstream pillar — the "gated" flag. Then set how much of each pillar's enabling work is actually delivered. The tool uses the same dependency engine as the HTR Simulator and the Friction Index, so a gate opens at the same threshold everywhere on the platform.

Expect the first run to be uncomfortable. Most organizations find components with no owner, components running ahead of gates nobody had named, and at least one piece of unblocked work that has been parked because its deadline felt distant. The value is not the verdicts themselves but the conversation they force: who has the authority to act on them, and is that authority real?

A useful test of whether the review is working comes from the book's advice to legislators and board members. Ask one question: which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? An organization running a genuine portfolio answers in a sentence. An organization running a list answers with a status summary of everything — which is itself the finding.

body.analogy: A kitchen does not start plating the main course because the dinner reservation is at eight; it starts when the sauce it depends on is ready. A good expediter watches what each dish is waiting on, not the clock on the wall — and moves cooks to whatever is holding everything else up.
body.concept: Scheduling by dependency rather than by deadline

points: A portfolio register — every component with a pillar, an owner, a type, a status, and a target — is a portfolio office's first deliverable, and it needs no software to build.
The sequencing test's verdicts change the conversation: a component behind a closed gate is correctly waiting, not behind schedule.
Only implementation waits for a gate; design work and care-model work that produces value on its own should run now (book Chapter 1).
In Vermont, Fall 2026, the test puts schedule pressure on the four unfinished Technology components and flags the AHS PMO itself as late by dependency order.
HealthCare.gov and Cover Oregon both lacked a single party owning integration; the federal site recovered within two months once one was in place, and Oregon moved to HealthCare.gov.
The risk register and the sequencing test should point at the same place; when they disagree, one of them is wrong.
A moderate risk score is not a licence to wait: social-risk adjustment scores 12 but has no upstream blocker and should already be running.

body.explanation: The test never uses the calendar target to decide a verdict. A component whose upstream gate is open and that is not running is late by dependency order, however distant its deadline — the same logic that flags the AHS PMO itself. "Correctly waiting" applies only when the upstream gate is closed.

options.text: It is correctly waiting, because its deadline is two years away
It is late by dependency order, because nothing upstream is holding it
It is running ahead of its gate
It cannot be assessed until the Economics gate opens

body.question: In the Vermont, Fall 2026 run of the sequencing test, the statewide AI-governance framework has a FY2028 adoption target and has not started. Its Technology gate is open. What does the test conclude?

summary: A hands-on companion to the book's Chapter 15: build a portfolio register, run the Portfolio Manager's four-step sequencing test against it, and read the verdicts alongside the risk register — worked on Vermont's 19 components and contrasted with the HealthCare.gov and Cover Oregon launches.
